#4306. 10 Pokémon That Are the Biggest Red Flags

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There are over 1,000 Pokémon now and they span nine generations of games. Over the years, there have been many Pokémon designs, with some of them being fantastic, and others being rather… questionable.

With that being said, everyone has a favorite Pokémon, but not all of them convey a positive or welcoming message. In fact, some of them are serious red flags to have as your favorite.

These Pokémon will make others cringe for obvious reasons, and possibly even question your taste. Sometimes it is about the Pokémon’s look, other times the Pokédex is to blame, and you can even blame society for others.

Charizard has been around since the beginning of the Pokémon series, and it quickly became a Pokémon that was beloved by everyone. Many of us were around to see Ash take in Charmander, and help it grow into a fiery beast.

However, there are many who consider Charizard to be a big red flag when choosing your favorite Pokémon. The reason for this is that you are far too basic if this is your choice.

Of course, there is a lot of context behind Charizard being a red flag. After all, it is the Pokémon that has received some of the most attention, with it getting multiple forms and promotions. It’s almost like Charizard is the mascot of Pokémon with how much attention it gets.

From the Eevee evolutions to Magikarp becoming something useful, here are the Pokémon in FireRed and LeafGreen that feel different after evolving.

The original generation of Pokémon was something that blew the minds of many kids. However, the magic that once created something that everyone loved ended up creating some rather poorly designed monsters in later generations.

One Pokémon design that felt uninspired is the Trubbish line, as it is nothing more than a bag of garbage that evolves into a pile of trash. Garbodor is nothing more than a trash pile that many associate with being smelly.

The internet ruined Garbodor by turning it into a meme where if you like the Pokémon, you are considered dirty. On the other hand, many associate this Pokémon as a red flag because choosing it feels like someone is purposefully trying to go against the grain by choosing a less universally loved Pokémon.

In past years, if you’d ask someone who their favorite Pokémon is, there was a large sect of the fan base that would say Typhlosion. He used to be cool, but everything changed when content was leaked that involved this once-innocent Pokémon.

As part of the leak in 2024, Typhlosion - specifically the Hisuian form - received some unsettling lore that involved folklore of it shapeshifting into a human and kidnapping a young girl. There’s more to it, but I don’t want to dive that deep.

Despite the leak never containing any canon information that made it into the games, and there being mistranslations, and other issues with it, Typhlosion has never really been able to escape the allegations, and so therefore, is still considered a red flag to many in the fan base.

When you bring together many people and give them the capability of being anonymous, as they can be on the internet, they have a habit of ruining everything you once loved. While there are multiple on this list, Lopunny is the first up.

Lopunny started off as Buneary - a rather adorable rabbit Pokémon - that gets an… interesting physique when it evolves into its final stage. Many saw this transformation, went online, and then proceeded to turn the Pokémon into a symbol for provocation.

Since then, it has been frowned upon whenever someone mentions that their favorite Pokémon is Lopunny, and the addition of Mega Lopunny did not help. Instead, it made things a bit worse.

Mr. Mime was an unsettling Pokémon when kids were introduced to it in the anime. Its human-like appearance mixed with a mime is something that is uncanny. However, it has only gotten worse over the years.

Digging through its Pokédex entries, you learn that it is capable of creating physical objects that are invisible. Along with that, if you interrupt its performance, it feels the need to slap you with its big flat hands.

This alone is weird, but you can add on the allegations that Mr. Mime is Ash’s stepfather in the anime. To cap it off, Mr. Mime got even more strange with the Detective Pikachu movie, further enhancing its uncanny and unsettling nature.

Did you choose Garchomp because you like the Pokémon, or did you choose it because it is a powerhouse and you are someone who gets overly competitive and sweaty during competition? Maybe it’s because you still have PTSD from Cynthia destroying you in Diamond and Pearl?

This is often what is associated with the love of Garchomp. There is no denying that Garchomp is an absolute beast of a Pokémon that can destroy others in competition, but that also makes many believe that those who like Garchomp have a far too competitive and aggressive mindset.

The other mindset people have is that Garchomp is associated with Cynthia from Diamond and Pearl. She dominated players in that era, and the idea is that those who like Garchomp haven’t gotten over that and want to inflict the same trauma on others.

There are Pokémon who have off Pokédex entries, with some of them being focused on some sort of trauma or horror story. Drifloon is one such Pokémon, with it being a ghost Pokémon who is known for kidnapping children.

The original Pokédex entries don’t make Drifloon out to be so bad, as the Dex says that it pulls on children to steal them away, but it ends up getting yanked around instead. However, this has gotten worse with time.

More recent entries specifically state that this Pokémon kidnaps children and whisks them off to the afterlife. Other entries talk about how it is specifically filled with souls and grows larger each time it steals one away. Let’s just leave this Pokémon out of our favorites list.

Pokemon Red/Blue's Lavender Town remains one of the eeriest creations in video gaming.

The internet has a way of taking any Pokémon that has slightly humanoid features and turning them into your worst nightmare. Similar to Lopunny before it, Gothitelle fell victim to those who seek to ruin things for other people.

Again, this is another Pokémon evolution line that starts off very innocent, with Gothita being a rather cute Pokémon that is very innocent in appearance. Unfortunately, that changes when it reaches its final evolution.

There is nothing innately wrong about liking this evolution line, but it definitely calls your taste into question, and many will immediately see the red flag fly, and it is completely understandable.

I am not sure that this even needs to be said because, of all the Pokémon with a humanoid appearance, Gardevoir has been treated the worst. Originally introduced in generation 3, the entire Raltz evolution line was loved, but then things went south very quickly.

Gardevoir is a Pokémon that resembles a woman in a flowing dress. Its body consists of said dress, which is more or less a flowing gown, and it has a hairstyle that appears to be done for a pageant or evening event.

However, this is enough to get the internet riled up, and Gardevoir was the first of the Pokémon of this style to be twisted by those who just seek to ruin things for other people. Now, this Pokémon is considered one of the biggest red flags of the franchise.

Eevee was, and still is, one of the most popular Pokémon there is, with many finding the little fox-like creature to be adorable. When it was introduced, it was beloved, and so were its original three evolutions; Flareon, Jolteon, and Vaporeon.

Unfortunately for Vaporeon, it became the fascination of one of the most perverse corners of the Pokémon fan base. So much so that it was treated far worse than Lopunny, Gothitelle, and Gardivoire combined.

The information about this Pokémon soon became a meme that spread like wildfire, leading to many victims being caught in the smoke. Now, many are ashamed to even talk about Vaporeon in a positive light, as it looks bad. What was once one of the most famous Pokémon of a generation has now become the biggest red flag in the fandom.

#4305. Free-To-Play MOBA Pokémon Unite Is Shutting Down In March

The free-to-play MOBA Pokémon Unite will shut down in March, over five years after its 2021 launch. Although a gradual suspension of services begins today, fans will enjoy one last hurrah thanks to a big in-game event running for the remainder of the game’s lifecycle.

Launched in July 2021 for Switch before migrating to iOS and Android later that year, Pokémon Unite was billed as a friendlier take on the MOBA genre popularized by Dota 2 and League of Legends, thanks to its short matches (10 minutes) and simplified mechanics. Despite its initial popularity, the game is winding down and will go offline for good on March 23, 2027.

An End of Service notice on the game’s website reads,

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021. We would like to express our thanks to everyone by holding a special event until service ends. The Pokémon Unite Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo competitive tournament (an event for Pokémon Unite only) will also be held as previously announced. We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service. After service ends, the 'Pokémon Unite Game Content Guidelines for Online Platforms' will no longer be published or maintained, and we will no longer provide support regarding use of Pokémon Unite videos and images.”

As of today, in-game sales of Aeos gems and Unite Club memberships/renewals have been suspended. Existing Unite Club members will continue to use their benefits until the end of the membership period.

On November 12, an update will kick off the aforementioned final special event, where players can obtain items such as all Unite licenses and Holoware that have appeared in the game up to that point. A library feature will also be added, letting players view certain records and in-game content even after the game shuts down on March 23. Those who don’t download the library feature before the shutdown date will not be able to get it afterward.

Qualifiers for the Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo Competitive tournament will take place as planned on December 5. After the game shuts down on March 23, players won't be able to log in to Pokémon Unite or play any battles. Only the library feature will remain accessible.

We enjoyed Pokémon Unite when it launched, with executive video editor Alex Van Aken scoring it an 8 out of 10 in his review, writing, “The game eats away the hours of my day as I reassuringly say to myself, 'Just one more match.' Battles play out with the spectacle that the Pokémon series is known for, and with so many abilities to choose from, no match feels the same as the last. The game’s simple mechanics and recognizable characters make for an approachable MOBA experience, and with a potential catalog of nearly 900 Pokémon to pick from, my hopes are high for the future of Pokémon Unite.”

Gentle Mates GC, on their Championship debut, beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo. The French-based side go into Sunday's best-of-five grand final with a two-map ban advantage, while Shopify Rebellion Gold must come through the lower final.

Gentle Mates GC are into the grand final of the VCT Game Changers Championship 2026. They beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo on Friday 30 October. The French-based side dropped the opening map and then took the next two. Both teams had arrived at the match with every map at the event won.

Shopify Rebellion Gold won map one, which lasted 53 minutes. On the second map they fought back to 10-10, but Gentle Mates closed it out 13-11 after 55 minutes. The decider on Summit ran for 57 minutes and finished 13-10 to Gentle Mates.

Coming through the upper bracket gives Gentle Mates a two-map ban advantage in the grand final. Shopify Rebellion Gold, led at the event by interim in-game leader alexis, drop into the lower bracket final against KRÜ Blaze.

This is Gentle Mates’ first appearance at the Championship. Their line-up of Marti, Nami, Wens, tokameite and berryx reached the upper final with 2-0 wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. Their last three EMEA Stage 3 results before the event were wins over G2 Gozen and SK Nebula, both 2-1, and a 3-2 defeat to G2 Gozen.

Shopify Rebellion Gold had cleared SK Nebula and KRÜ Blaze without losing a map. Before travelling, they beat FlyQuest RED 3-1 and 2-1 and SwimTrek Blue 2-0 in North America Stage 2. At last year’s Championship in Seoul, Team Liquid Brazil beat them 3-2 in the title match.

#4303. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4298. Phantom Blade Zero Review – Wuxia Wonder Abounds

Rooted in Wuxian storytelling and scale, built on an impressively detailed combat system, and wrapped in a bloody Chinese martial underground that’s a genuine joy to play in, Phantom Blade Zero is a feat. It joins an echelon of action pedigree that includes Sekiro, Devil May Cry, Bayonetta, and just about any other action game you hold in high regard. It hails from developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile and smaller-scale games, and I’m shocked by what it’s pulled off with its triple-A action inauguration. But make no mistake: though Phantom Blade Zero is this team’s first crack at a game like this, it is an incredibly confident, strong debut.

Protagonist Soul is a stoic martial arts master betrayed by the Order he’s sworn his life to; he dies and returns to life with only 66 days to live. That’s enough time to settle his debts, repay his betrayers, and end a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the Wulin realm. This narrative is Phantom Blade Zero's weakest link, but its premise adds enough mystery and tension to keep this Wuxian journey exciting through to its final, realm-shattering moments. Narrative bombshells drop not just through the game’s general fantasy-realism art direction, but also through anime scenes, opera puppet shows, animated brushstroke sequences, and more, highlighting Chinese culture and its integral place in Phantom Blade Zero.

The game features a staggering number of unique enemy types, and though the final hours get a bit repetitive, it’s admirable how long S-Game maintains such a high level of combat-oriented ecstasy. Soul’s access to weapons drives that exhilaration. Every weapon is wholly unique. Because the combat is combo-based, picking up a new weapon feels like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. Each has its own moveset and abilities, with later-game weapons featuring combo lists that look more at home in a Street Fighter menu. Add in the special, tide-turning weapons known as Phantom Edges, with limited charge-based uses, and there’s no shortage of permutations to delightfully experiment with.

Drawing on Chinese cinema, Phantom Blade Zero's setpiece bosses boast a sense of awe and scale only the genre's best typically offer. With virtually no repeat bosses, save for a few in separate trials, it’s impressive how many powerful figures I flayed, and how many delivered a unique fight. I also appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases, as they remove the frustrating repetition of replaying phase one again and again just to take another stab at the second phase I’m struggling with.

You’d be forgiven for assuming Phantom Blade Zero is a Soulslike, given its challenging bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, this game’s equivalent of bonfires. It definitively isn’t, though. The challenge is much more surmountable; the game isn’t interested in making you die over and over, there are difficulty options, and you can equip accessories to make parries and dodges easier. World progression is materially different, too, as enemies don’t respawn after you kill them. It’s an interesting, perhaps blasphemous, choice for the genre, but it's surprisingly effective, adding a sense of worldbuilding and tangible progression I didn’t know I wanted from my action games. Soul is on a mission to remove evil, and mechanically, I’m doing just that. Enemies don’t respawn incoherently just because I heal and save.

Environmental features weave in and out of each other, and the architectural design and layout of these regions lead to many subsequent “aha” moments. S-Game infuses search-action elements into this exploration through the aforementioned Phantom Edges, some of which double as tools to unlock surprising new areas in both new and previously visited biomes. As a result, backtracking and exploration remain fresh. A lot of it is optional, as are some of Phantom Blade Zero's most rewarding elements, including its demanding “perfect” ending. Sadly, this renders other endings unsatisfying, with clear chunks intentionally missing.

Despite forays into the Uncanny Valley, Phantom Blade Zero is visually striking, and the action is brilliantly animated. It’s all set to genre-breaking music, too, with original metalcore songs, operatic choirs, 808s, and traditional Chinese instrumentation, creating a score as illustrious as the action it enhances.

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding action achievement, almost unbelievably so for a game that is essentially a studio’s genre debut. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, one that recognizes the genre’s strengths and weaknesses and addresses both with fantastical Wuxian style. Though the action genre is always jam-packed with new releases, few are as special as Phantom Blade Zero.

#4297. 10 Soulslikes That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Creating a new genre is quite difficult, and while that's not exactly what FromSoftware did, it certainly gave rise to a new generation of titles aptly categorized under the Soulslike label.

The reasons why this phenomenon emerged organically and without premeditation are plentiful, as are the numerous gems that its rise to popularity among developers has gifted us.

Gradually, the niche became a popular segment among creators and players, but even so, its expansion has been such that many creations, despite their quality, have flown under the radar of most.

Therefore, in order to give due recognition to those works that oscillate between being unknown and not properly appreciated, I invite you to read this list of ten Soulslikes that are unexpected masterpieces.

As a self-proclaimed devotee of boss rushes, especially given that they're always the most interesting aspect of any Soulslike, no amount of praise is enough to highlight Rubinite's current popularity.

Despite its branching nature, it features an engaging story that perfectly complements the gameplay, which isn't the sole focus of the title; rather, both elements work together to create a truly well-rounded experience.

However, it's clear that anyone playing Rubinite will do so for the bosses (or for its gorgeous pixel art), and in this department, it performs sensationally, with varied adversaries in both aesthetics and gimmicks that truly maximize the game's satisfying mechanics.

As one of the year's best indie games, it inevitably makes the list of the most outstanding Soulslikes, especially since it pleasantly surprised me even though I'd been eagerly awaiting its release since the day it was announced.

The so-called flow state is a subtle key to the excellence of a Soulslike, as the magnificent AI LIMIT demonstrates through its simple yet direct combat that truly manages to captivate you from the first touch.

I admit I'm usually wary of titles that share its visual style due to past bad experiences, though this game reversed my expectations with its solid gameplay, both in its design and execution.

AI LIMIT's game feel is the experience's highlight, with mesmerizing encounters that, while not at the most challenging end, strike a perfect balance between being challenging and never frustrating.

If your mind, like mine, unconsciously compares it to similar products within and outside Soulslikes, I recommend you completely dispel any doubts, as few other examples of the genre can offer this level of reward.

If you remember the feeling you had the first time you played a Soulsborne game, that pleasant wonder of being captivated as you discovered an expansive world brimming with majesty, then encountering Mohrta is a gift from heaven.

Despite the obvious gameplay differences, since the game is both an FPS and an ARPG, the sense of discovery is practically the same, generating indescribable joy when you come across a new weapon, enemy, area, or NPC.

Everything in the game is so bizarre yet charming that it's difficult to play it in short bursts, because what it really makes you want to do is burn the midnight oil while enjoying its unparalleled inventiveness in terms of story, worldbuilding, and design.

If you've played any other title from its developer, Scumhead, you can more or less imagine what Mohrta has in store, though I can already tell you that it's the best video game this eccentric creator has ever produced.

There's nothing more fitting for this season than being destroyed by the same boss fifty-seven times in a row.

While I always found Mortal Shell a fascinating exercise in imagination within a dark and obtuse fantasy setting, I always considered it merely good, nothing more, but I can't say the same for Mortal Shell II.

Coming from a first title that was rough around the edges and failed to fully convince, Cold Symmetry surpassed even the most optimistic predictions with a sequel that addresses its predecessor's every single flaw.

The enemies' legibility, ease of spatial awareness, combat's feel, orientation within the main content, level design's firmness... It's comparatively much more robust, and I'd be lying if I said I expected such a significant leap in quality.

Therefore, Mortal Shell II proved me wrong, and nothing could make me happier. That it belongs in the discussion of the best Soulslikes of all time is undeniable at this point, yet it doesn't rank higher on the list because I'm sure there were devotees who knew this would be the outcome.

Bloodborne is the kind of video game that, once you finish it, leaves you with the bittersweet feeling that you'll never experience anything like it again, but Vigil: The Longest Night comes pretty close.

Although its gameplay is much more tactical and careful than its 3D counterpart, its atmosphere is undeniably analogous, especially due to the artistic and narrative similarities that place both within the realm of cosmic and body horror.

From there on, the comparisons begin to diminish, as it's more reminiscent of Salt and Sanctuary in its combat and progression systems, though its founding elements are masterfully aligned with FromSoftware's prodigious child.

Therefore, Vigil: The Longest Night achieves a feat that very few others can: making you feel like you're playing Bloodborne. This might seem like a weak argument for calling it a masterpiece, but when you truly grasp the difficulty of such an undertaking, it's not so far-fetched after all.

If you haven't played Queen's Domain yet, be sure to leave this article open in another tab while you download it, because one of the most immersive games of 2026 awaits you.

If King's Field were released today, I'm sure it would strive to resemble the work of Freshly Baked Games LLC, whom I was honored to discover through their debut title, The New Flesh, and with whom I've been inseparable ever since.

The decision to follow their lead was the right one, as keeping an eye out for the release of their retro-fantasy action RPG has given me one of the year's finest experiences, especially since I love titles inspired by Dark Souls more for their level design, interconnectivity, and progression than for their combat systems.

Some might say that Queen's Domain isn't Soulslike enough because it aligns more with the philosophy than the practicalities, but for me, that's enough, as it's one of the most highly recommended and captivating games released in the last couple of months.

In these Soulslikes, studying your enemy and playing carefully is vital.

Soulslikes tend to be very traditional in terms of what they do and how they do it, but the arrival of an outsider to the genre like One More Level brought a breath of fresh air in the form of Valor Mortis.

As the creators of Ghostrunner, a first-person platformer that excels in its spectacular movement sequences, their ARPG inherited that skill to create the most enjoyable experience in the genre in terms of movement.

The levels are gigantic in scale and verticality, allowing you to fly through the air using a grappling hook, run along walls, and swing to ledges, giving it a completely unique feel that no other Soulslike has ever achieved.

Add to that combat that balances parries and dodges like Lies of P, spectacular and grotesque (though easy) bosses, and customization options that are limited but refined, and you realize that Valor Mortis is much more than what people say about it.

Considering they had just released the least-reviewed Darksiders game to date, nobody bet a penny on Gunfire Games' success with Remnant: From the Ashes, and yet nobody remained silent when it came to praising its remarkable quality.

Making a permanently cooperative title with third-person shooter mechanics in a sporadically online and predominantly melee branch is among the boldest moves the genre has ever seen, which is already quite an achievement.

Regardless, Remnant: From the Ashes doesn't stand out simply for its innovation; it's a robust and extremely fun game whose variety of weapons, bosses, and environments allows for a deep adventure, brimming with content that's worth experiencing in its entirety.

Its breakout performance is a bit of a blow to me, as I suspect that, over the years, they'll prioritize this IP over Darksiders, but if that's the sacrifice to keep getting the best co-op games in the genre... so be it.

The First Berserker: Khazan's announcement certainly didn't leave any avid fan indifferent, as it gave the impression of being a major beast within the genre, but I don't think anyone could have anticipated its true severity.

Although its average critical reception is more mixed, I'm more inclined to agree with the unanimous opinion of the gaming community that it's a serious contender to be FromSoftware's ultimate heir.

It's difficult to describe what you have to feel to comprehend it truly, but holding the controls while fighting The First Berserker: Khazan's bosses is an untamed magic that courses through your entire body, filling you with adrenaline and excitement that are tough to match.

Were it not for the somewhat simplistic nature of its basic enemies and environments, the discussion about the title would be very different, yet you forget all of that when you enter the zone of maximum concentration thanks to its diverse, refined, and satisfying gameplay.

Every genre has its defining features, and the Soulslike is one that gets misunderstood fairly often with games like these blurring the line.

The only reason I disagree with those who believe the previous Soulslike is the best of them all is due to Lies of P's existence, a title that no one even came close to predicting, even if today it is commonly recognized under said distinction.

When we talk about unexpected masterpieces, the fact that NEOWIZ, a company originally conceived to distribute music games for the PlayStation Portable, developed the only Soulslike capable of rivaling the originals is among the entire century's most unpredictable events.

No matter how much faith you had in its release, there was no way to imagine that Lies of P would have such a vast arsenal, iconic and demandingly engaging bosses, levels crafted to perfection, a spectacular soundtrack, and even a story that keeps you engaged until the very last second.

Add to that its worldbuilding, side quests, flawless combination of parries and dodges, level of customization through the weapon assembly system, masterful enemy positioning and shortcuts... and you're left with a title that can only be described as majestic.

Lies of P raised the bar for the genre to a new level, and since 2024, it has become the ultimate benchmark despite coming from such a modest and distant background as that of its creators.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

Paper Rex has broken up the core of its VALORANT roster. The Singapore organisation is parting with its captain and one of its best-known players as the 2027 season approaches. d4v41 had been with Paper Rex since its founding in 2020. He played first on its CS:GO roster, then moved with the team to VALORANT. Jinggg joined on 28 September 2021.

Neither player has named a destination. In the farewell video Paper Rex released, d4v41 said he was moving to a new team. Jinggg wrote on X that he was excited about what comes next. d4v41 also asked fans to keep supporting the organisation after both have gone.

The split follows a season that faded at the end. Paper Rex were runners-up at both Masters Santiago and Masters London earlier in 2026. At Champions in Shanghai, they lost 2-0 to LOUD in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 7 October. A 2-1 defeat to T1 in lower-bracket round one ended their run on 9 October. The event carried a $2,250,000 prize pool. LOUD went on to beat Team Vitality in the final.

The pair leave with a long record together. Jinggg helped Paper Rex to second place at Masters Copenhagen 2022. He was also part of the run to the Champions 2023 final, where the team were runners-up. Liquipedia lists both players in the line-up that won VCT 2025 Masters Toronto.

The changes are not forced by the league. The organisation is owned by IMPLS Entertainment Pte Ltd. Riot has cut the number of partner teams in each region from ten to eight for 2027–28. That leaves 32 across the four regions.

The Pacific format rewards that security. The eight partners receive seeded places at Kickoff in January 2027. Four further places go to teams that come through open qualifiers. Paper Rex can therefore reshape its roster without needing to qualify.

Two Masters winners on the open market could matter well beyond the Pacific. EMEA’s eight partners for 2027 are Fnatic, BBL Esports, FUT Esports, Team Heretics, Team Liquid, Gentle Mates, Karmine Corp and Team Vitality. Under Riot’s open qualifier rules, most regions require three of a team’s five players to come from that region. Teams must also keep three of five players between events to carry their progress forward. Those limits will frame how far any club can rebuild around new signings.

Neither TYLOO nor Lynn Vision is expected to play again before the cutoff. That leaves the Asian race effectively over.

The Lisbon event was a Valve Tier 2 tournament run by Hyped and PEW PEW. It ran from 29 October to 1 November with 13 teams and a prize pool of €12,187.50. Groups were GSL-format best-of-threes, followed by single-elimination best-of-three playoffs. TYLOO are listed in joint fifth to eighth place.

IEM Beijing is a far bigger draw on paper. ESL is staging it from 2 to 8 November at the Bloomage Biotech Biohyalux ECM Arena. It is S-Tier and Valve Tier 1, with 16 teams playing for $1,250,000.

#4292. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4291. Nintendo Indie World Showcase Recap: Everything We Saw

The year is nearing its conclusion, and the last big AAA titles are rolling out one-by-one. But today, it was all about the independent titles on Nintendo's latest Indie World Showcase, highlighting new games from smaller indie teams coming to the Switch and Switch 2.

Here's everything we saw at the October 2026 Nintendo Indie World Showcase.

Today's Indie World Showcase started with a big headliner, as the long-awaited witch-life simulator Witchbrook got a release date. Chucklefish and Robtality's cozy magical world goes live on January 28, 2027.

Fans of 3D platformers should probably keep an eye on Winds of Viridia, which looks like a colorful game with a lot of interesting movement and exploration. Shark Jump's fantastical platformer is arriving next year, but if the wait's too long, a free demo is coming today on the eShop.

From one of the co-creators of Celeste, City of None has a gorgeous pixelated art style and colors that immediately remind me of Game Boy Color classics. It's a 2D platformer where you leap around, fight enemies, and explore the strange city around you. The jumping and fighting look solid, and I really like the mysterious atmosphere and art direction. City of None's set for sometime in 2027.

The sword-surfing adventure from the makers of Abzu and Journey is coming to Nintendo Switch 2 on October 29, 2026 - tomorrow! It's a gorgeous adventure that earned a Must-Play badge from us, so it's worth your time if you like the kinds of gorgeous, beautiful adventures Giant Squid (developer of Abzu) is known for.

Take an overhead camera angle, brawler gameplay, and some John Wick sensibilities, and you've got Tenjutsu, a stylish roguelike where you use your martial arts prowess to tear apart crime syndicates. I really enjoy the look and vibe of this one, and it's from one of the designers of Dead Cells, too. Tenjutsu might be one to keep an eye on when it arrives on Switch 2 in 2027.

RPG fans have been eating well, and it looks like the feast could continue next year with Threads of Time. The time-traveling RPG is coming to both Switch and Switch 2 next summer, and it's looking absolutely gorgeous.

Ah, raccoons. Nature's most adorable little scamps. If you and your friends have ever wanted to live out the dream of being a rambunctious band of raccoons wreaking havoc on the town, Dumpster Gang sets out to give you just that fantasy in March 2027.

I've already enjoyed quite a bit of Super Battle Golf on PC, so I'll tell you now: if you enjoy golf games and want some Mario Party annoy-your-friends antics wound around them, Super Battle Golf should be on your radar for its March 25, 2027 launch on Switch 2.

From the makers of Cozy Grove, this multiplayer game encourages players to build a home above the clouds with friends and explore the world around them. Spirit Crossing looks like a big world to make your own alongside your pals, starting November 16, 2026 on both Switch and Switch 2.

Want something a little sillier? My Arms Are Longer Now is a game about, well, really long arms. With numerous Australian comedians lending their vocal talents to the project, this seems like it could be a quirky, charming, and delightfully funny experience when it arrives on both Switch and Switch 2 on March 11, 2027.

Raccoin: Chaos Max Edition hits Switch 2 on November 10, 2026, and a free demo is out later today.

#4290. Jordan Esports Federation signs MoU with King Hussein Business Park to host more events

Priya Venkatesh has been following the money in esports since before brand deals were considered legitimate marketing. She got pulled into the scene through competitive fighting games and eventually found herself more interested in the contracts and partnerships behind the tournaments than the matches themselves. These days she focuses on how brands navigate esports sponsorships, where the smart money is going, and which deals are actually built to last versus the ones that look good in a press release.

The Jordan Esports Federation (JEF) has signed a memorandum of understanding with King Hussein Business Park (KHBP) in Amman, giving the national body a formal framework to stage more tournaments and events at the site it already calls home.

KHBP announced the deal on Sunday in a statement published on its website. Prince Omar bin Faisal, who is President of the JEF, attended the signing.

Under the MoU, the federation and the business park will jointly host and organise specialised competitions on the KHBP campus. They will also receive the international delegations and official guests that travel to those events. Beyond the competitive side, the two organisations plan to cooperate on media and marketing, look at shared education, training and community projects, and swap knowledge and expertise.

Neither party has disclosed financial terms or the length of the agreement.

KHBP CEO Eng. Ammar Ezzeddin presented the MoU as part of the park’s wider ambitions. “This partnership builds on our ongoing efforts to create an enabling environment for institutions, initiatives and high-potential sectors, and to establish KHBP as a hub for innovation and technology,” he said.

He added: “We look forward to helping the sector thrive and to hosting more tournaments and events that put Jordanian talent in the spotlight and raise the Kingdom’s profile in this field.”

JEF Vice President Hazem Bawab focused on the competitive and grassroots goals. “This partnership is a significant step in our drive to develop the esports industry in Jordan and elevate the standard of local, regional and international competitions and activities,” he said.

Bawab continued: “We look forward to drawing on the setup and capabilities that KHBP offers to scale our work, nurture young talent and launch joint programmes that help the industry grow and encourage greater participation.”

The deal formalises a relationship that already exists on the ground. According to The Esports Radar, the JEF, which is the government recognised regulator for esports in the country, is based at the park in West Amman.

A lot of that work happens at THE ARC, the arena and gaming dome inside the park. The same report lists past events there including the fourth Arab Esports League, a Women’s Esports Championship and Red Bull Login, which doubled as Jordan’s national final stage in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. The venue is also an incubation centre supported by the federation and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, and runs training camps for players hoping to turn professional.

KHBP has been a destination for esports investment for some time. In 2024, lounge operator True Gamers announced plans for an esports venue in Jordan at the business park, a project in which its CPO publicly thanked the JEF and Prince Omar.

The timing also puts Amman in the industry spotlight. PocketGamer.biz points out that Pocket Gamer Connects Jordan takes place on 7 and 8 November, bringing many of the region’s games industry stakeholders to the city later this week.

#4289. 10 Best GameCube JRPGs That You Need to Play in Fall 2026

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

There’s always a specific moment every year where I realise that autumn has properly arrived. The evenings start drawing in before I’ve even had the chance to notice, the air gets crisper, and my coffee suddenly needs to be hot enough to warm both hands around the mug. I don’t think of myself as someone who hibernates, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t naturally start staying in a little more this time of year.

And honestly? I love it. Being cozied up on my sofa with a blanket, a hot drink and the rain doing its thing outside is one of my favourite feelings, and it always seems to pull me towards games that tug on my nostalgia heartstrings. More often than not, that means the GameCube. Its JRPG library was smaller than what you’d find on its competitors, but it was stranger, braver and far more charming than it ever got credit for.

So many GameCube games have managed to escape the console in some way, but there are some JRPGs still waiting to abandon ship.

Some of these games have since found their way onto modern hardware, whilst others are still very much living in 2004, waiting for you to dig out an old memory card. A couple of them are certified classics, a few are delightfully weird, and at least one asks you to keep a close eye on the expiry date of your bananas. So grab a blanket, put the kettle on, and let’s take a look at the ten GameCube JRPGs that deserve a spot in your autumn rotation.

Tales of Symphonia was a big deal for GameCube owners. Released in Japan in August 2003, before reaching North America in July 2004 and Europe that November, it was the first Tales game to make the jump into 3D, complete with gorgeous cel-shaded visuals and character designs by Kosuke Fujishima. You follow Lloyd Irving and his childhood friend Colette, the Chosen One, on a journey to regenerate the dying world of Sylvarant. Naturally, things turn out to be a lot more complicated than that.

What made it really special, though, was the multiplayer. Up to four people could plug in a controller and take over a party member in the real-time battles, even if the camera stubbornly stuck to player one, leaving everyone else to fend for themselves off-screen. Add in the optional skits you could trigger with the Z button and a soundtrack by Motoi Sakuraba, and you have a game that will happily eat 80 hours of your autumn. If digging out the original hardware isn’t for you, the 2023 remaster on Switch, PS4 and Xbox One is the easier way in.

Taking a franchise famous for its tight, side-scrolling action and turning it into a turn-based RPG sounds like a recipe for disaster. Capcom did it anyway in 2004, and the result is a wonderfully fun little oddity that also found its way onto the PlayStation 2. Set in the 23rd century, X, Zero and newcomer Shadow are sent to Giga City to put an end to a Reploid rebellion led by Epsilon, with everything revolving around a powerful new substance called Force Metal.

Battles are snappy, and Hyper Modes, which let your characters transform mid-fight for a temporary power boost, keep things from ever getting stale. Axl joins the fold along the way, as does a slick bounty hunter called Spider, and the cast as a whole has a lot more personality than I expected going in. It received a fairly average critical response at the time, but it sold well, and I think it has aged far better than its reputation suggests.

Baten Kaitos was developed by Monolith Soft and tri-Crescendo, published by Namco, and released in Japan in December 2003, before making its way west across 2004 and 2005. Its world is made up of islands floating high in the sky, with the oceans below reduced to nothing more than legend. Fittingly, the name comes from the Arabic for “belly of the whale”, and it’s also the name of a star in the constellation Cetus. You don’t play as the protagonist, Kalas, but as a Guardian Spirit bonded to him, and he will very happily talk to you directly.

Everything revolves around Magnus, cards that capture the essence of objects, and with over 1,000 of them, deck building gets intricate fast. The fun part? Many Magnus change in real time. Grapes go rotten, then turn into wine, then vinegar, and a perfectly good banana will eventually turn on you if you leave it sitting in your deck. The 2023 HD Remaster on Switch bundles it with its prequel, Baten Kaitos Origins, which is a lovely excuse to finally experience both.

Path of Radiance launched in 2005 as the ninth main entry in the series, but only the third to make it to the West. It was the first Fire Emblem on a home console since Thracia 776, and it brought a few firsts along with it: 3D maps, voice acting and full motion cutscenes. You take control of Ike, a young mercenary who ends up at the centre of a war on the continent of Tellius, where the human beorc and the half-human laguz share a long, complicated history of mistrust.

Ike went on to become one of the series’ most beloved characters, joining the roster of Super Smash Bros. Brawl and later topping the men’s side of the very first Choose Your Legends poll in Fire Emblem Heroes. Permadeath is, of course, still very much a thing, so be prepared for heartbreak if you get careless. Players with save data from the Game Boy Advance Fire Emblem games could even link up to unlock concept art and special maps, which is the kind of connectivity I often find myself missing nowadays.

For years, a physical copy cost an arm and a leg. Thankfully, it joined the GameCube library on Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in January 2026, so if you own a Switch 2, there has never been an easier time to sign up with the Greil Mercenaries. And should you get hooked, Radiant Dawn on the Wii picks up the story afterwards.

Skies of Arcadia first set sail on the Dreamcast in 2000, but for many of us, Legends on the GameCube was where we first met Vyse, Aika and Fina. You play as a Blue Rogue, essentially a sky pirate with a moral compass, in a world of floating continents orbited by six moons. The Valuan Empire is hunting down the Moon Crystals, and it falls to you and your crew to stop them, mostly by being extremely charming about it.

Exploration is at the heart of everything. Sailing into the unknown, stumbling across Discoveries and selling the information for a reward is ridiculously satisfying, and Legends bumped the total up to 89. The port also added Moonfish to hunt down and a bounty hunter named Piastol, whose side story finally explains how Vyse got that scar on his face. Crucially, it also toned down the random encounter rate, which anyone who survived the Dreamcast version will deeply appreciate.

If you're looking for some rough times on the Gamecube, here are 8 hard to beat Gamecube JRPGs.

Long before Demon’s Souls, FromSoftware made a card-based action RPG for the GameCube. Known as Rune in Japan, Lost Kingdoms released there in April 2002, with Activision publishing it in North America and Europe later that year. It was one of the very first JRPGs on the GameCube, and it shows in the best possible way: it’s a little rough, a little ambitious, and absolutely its own thing.

You play as Princess Katia, tasked with saving the five kingdoms of Argwyll from a mysterious fog that is swallowing the land. Instead of swinging a sword, you build a deck of cards, each one summoning a creature or weapon in real time, which makes every encounter feel like a frantic little puzzle. There’s even a two-player mode where you can pit your deck against a friend’s.

Reviews were average at the time, but it did well enough to get a sequel, Lost Kingdoms II, set 200 years later. Looking back now, it’s fascinating to see the studio already leaning into melancholy, fog-drenched fantasy a whole seven years before it would change everything. It’s not the most polished game on this list, but it might just be the most interesting.

The Thousand-Year Door released in 2004 and is still, for many, the high point of the Paper Mario series. After Princess Peach sends Mario a treasure map and promptly goes missing, he ends up in Rogueport, a rather grimy town sitting on top of a legendary door, and sets out to find the seven Crystal Stars. Along the way, you’ll pick up a wonderful cast of partners, from know-it-all Goombella to Admiral Bobbery, a retired sailor who just so happens to be a Bob-omb.

Battles take place on a literal stage in front of an audience, who can cheer you on, throw items at you or bring the set crashing down. Every chapter feels like a different genre, whether that’s climbing the ranks in the Glitz Pit wrestling arena or solving a whodunnit aboard the Excess Express. Meanwhile, Peach is on her own little adventure with a computer called TEC-XX, and the interludes where you take control of Bowser are pure comedic gold. If you’d rather not hunt down a GameCube copy, the 2024 Switch remake is a gorgeous way to play.

Pokémon Colosseum turned the formula on its head. There are no wild Pokémon to catch, no gyms to conquer, and instead of a wide-eyed kid, you play as Wes, a former member of Team Snagem who kicks off the game by blowing up their hideout. Set in the desert region of Orre, you use a Snag Machine to steal Shadow Pokémon, whose hearts have been closed off by Team Cipher, straight from other trainers.

Every battle is a double battle, you start with Espeon and Umbreon, and slowly purifying your Shadow Pokémon by fighting alongside them is a surprisingly heartfelt gameplay loop. In North America, pre-ordering the game got you a bonus disc that let you send a Jirachi to your copy of Ruby or Sapphire, which also fixed the infamous berry glitch. Europe, sadly, didn’t get one.

It sold 2.41 million copies worldwide, and its sequel, Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, joined the Switch 2’s GameCube library earlier this year. Colosseum was announced for the same service back in April 2025, and as of writing, we are still waiting for a release date. Patience is a virtue, or so they keep telling me.

Evolution Worlds is a curious one. Developed by Sting and published by Ubisoft outside of Japan, it arrived in 2002 as a compilation of two Dreamcast games, packing an abbreviated version of Evolution: The World of Sacred Device and the full Evolution 2: Far Off Promise onto one GameCube disc. Both games also received newly recorded English voice acting.

You play as Mag Launcher, a young adventurer exploring ancient ruins with a Cyframe, a powerful tool left behind by a long-lost civilisation. At its core, this is a turn-based dungeon crawler, and a genuinely charming one at that. It also has some of the most gloriously unhinged character names I’ve ever come across: Mag is joined by Linear Cannon, Chain Gun, Pepper Spray and his ever-loyal butler, Gre Nade.

I won’t pretend it’s the deepest game on this list. It really isn’t. But sometimes all you want on a rainy evening is a straightforward dungeon crawl with a lot of heart, and Evolution Worlds delivers exactly that. It’s comfort food in JRPG form, and there’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles was a big moment, being the first Final Fantasy on a Nintendo home console since Final Fantasy VI back in 1994. Its world is covered in a poisonous miasma, and every village relies on a crystal to keep it at bay. Once a year, each village sends out a caravan to collect myrrh from distant trees, carrying a crystal chalice to protect them along the way, which many fans affectionately call the bucket.

The real hook was its multiplayer, and the price tag that came with it. Up to four players could join in, but every single one of them needed a Game Boy Advance and a link cable to act as their controller and personal screen. It was ambitious, a little bit impractical, and an absolute blast if you managed to pull it off. Playing solo, a Moogle carries the chalice for you instead.

You create your own caravanner from one of four tribes, the Clavat, Lilty, Yuke or Selkie, and set off into a world that rewards slow, patient journeys. If wrangling four GBAs sounds like a bit much, the 2020 Remastered Edition added online multiplayer, so your friends can join from the comfort of their own sofas. The myrrh only needs collecting once a year, after all.

Even though the GameCube didn't have a massive library, it did feature several fun and ambitious JRPG adventures.

#4288. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4286. KRÜ Blaze win Game Changers Championship from lower bracket, ending Gentle Mates’ unbeaten run

KRÜ Blaze came through the lower bracket to beat Europe's Gentle Mates GC over five maps in São Paulo, giving LATAM its first Game Changers Championship title. They are also the last winners of the standalone event, as next year's final moves to Champions.

KRÜ Blaze are the 2026 VALORANT Game Changers Championship winners. They edged Gentle Mates GC 3-2 at the Riot Games Arena in São Paulo on 1 November. No Latin American team had lifted the title before. No team had ever won it from the lower bracket either.

The event ran from 22 October, with 10 teams competing. Gentle Mates earned US$100,000 as runners-up. Shopify Rebellion Gold took US$70,000 for third place and MIBR GC US$50,000 for fourth.

KRÜ took the long route. They beat Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 23 October. A 2-0 loss to Shopify Rebellion Gold on 27 October then dropped them into the lower bracket. They answered with clean sweeps of Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. On 31 October they beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 3-1 in the best-of-five lower-bracket final.

The grand final swung back and forth. Gentle Mates took Haven 13-5 before KRÜ levelled on Abyss by the same score. KRÜ led the third map 10-2 at half-time. Gentle Mates fought back, but KRÜ closed it out 14-12 in overtime. Gentle Mates then won Split 13-8 to force a decider. KRÜ led 11-5 on Ascent and won it by the same margin as Split.

Liquipedia named KRÜ’s Argentine player tok1o as the event’s MVP. Brazilian teammates antG and none became the first Brazilians to win an international tournament held in São Paulo.

The result breaks a pattern. Before 2026 the title went to G2 Gozen for Europe in 2022, Shopify Rebellion for North America in 2023 and 2024, and Team Liquid Brazil in 2025. KRÜ’s own record at the event had improved steadily. They finished 7th–8th in 2022 and 5th–6th in each of the next two years. Last year they came fourth.

For European fans, it was a painful near miss. Gentle Mates GC arrived as EMEA’s top seed on circuit points. The team had not lost a series in São Paulo before the final, according to Esports News UK.

It capped a strong debut season in the circuit. Gentle Mates won EMEA Stage 1 by sweeping G2 Gozen 3-0 on 22 February. They lost the Stage 2 final to SK Nebula on 24 May without winning a map. On 30 August they lost the Stage 3 final to G2 Gozen in a fifth map. Silver in São Paulo leaves them with one title from four finals this year.

— VCT Pacific (@vctpacific) November 1, 2026

The São Paulo final also closes a format. KRÜ are the last team to lift the trophy at a separate event of its own. For the first time, the Game Changers Championship will finish at Champions. Under Riot’s 2027 plan, non-partner teams that qualify for the Game Changers Championship will receive an extra US0,000 incentive. VALORANT Champions 2027 is scheduled for 16 September to 10 October in Austin.

#4281. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4279. Here's The Best Graphics And Performance Mode For Phantom Blade Zero On PlayStation 5

Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review. That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.

However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.

Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced, which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.

The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.

Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!
