#4250. PlayStation Announces New Portal Model With Internal Storage

The PlayStation Portal is low-key one of the biggest wins the Sony studio has pulled off during this back half of the PS5 generation. A handheld device that it continues to update to the point that it’s far better than the product that launched three years ago. Those updates keep on coming too, with the biggest one yet just announced. The trouble is, there’s a catch. Well, actually, there are a few of them.

Announced via the PlayStation Blog, a new model of the Midnight Black PS Portal is being released on December 10, 2026. The first catch, and it’s the biggest of them all, is that this new model will only be released in Japan.

The new Portal will cost 39,980 yen, so around $250, which is the same amount as a standard model currently costs in the US. It comes with a month of PS Plus Premium, the subscription tier you need to stream games directly from the Cloud to your Portal without being tethered to a PS5.

Since so much has changed about the PS Portal, we've re-reviewed it to determine whether it's still worth buying in 2026.

The blog post even notes that the Portal is the perfect way to play PS5 games without owning a console, which is the first time I’ve seen PlayStation push that agenda, even though an update has made that possible on all Portals. It has even changed the device’s name, starting with this new model, from PlayStation Portal Remote Player to simply PlayStation Portal Player.

It’s a note towards the end of the post that sets this new model apart from the older ones, and is why a whole new model needs to be released rather than simply rolling out an update for pre-existing ones. “Furthermore, with an eye towards future functionality, the new model includes additional internal storage,” the blog reads.

Even though the new Portal’s release is only a month away, it adds that more details will be revealed about the device’s new storage capabilities when they’re finalized. The implication of that is the new Portal will actually be able to have a game or two stored on it that can be played anywhere. No PS5 tether needed, and perhaps no WiFi connection needed to stream games from the Cloud either.

There is a healthy, and warranted, amount of skepticism surrounding what exactly the internal storage comment might mean. If it means what it implies, then the Portal takes one step closer to becoming a standalone PlayStation handheld.

That seems unlikely, though, unless the Portal has been completely overhauled and is somehow now able to run games without the help of streaming. This also feels like another way to get more people into the PlayStation ecosystem without making new consoles. The reason PlayStation doesn’t want to make new consoles right now is because RAM and storage cost a fortune, so putting a significant amount of it into these new Portals feels like an odd move.

An estimate based on how many PS5 owners have used one has been calculated.

#4249. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.

#4248. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

#4245. 8 Nintendo Titles That Should Get The Ocarina of Time Remake Treatment

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games ever created. Fans of this game talk about it with passion, remembering it as a key part of their childhood. The remake shows that fans still love this title, even almost 30 years after the original’s release. It also introduces new features and controls.

Of course, this isn’t the only game that Nintendo has ever made. Nintendo is known for creating many timeless games that fans continue to go back to year after year.

While they may not be as beloved as Ocarina of Time, these games definitely deserve to get the same treatment, breathing new life into them.

Super Mario Sunshine is one of those Nintendo titles that divides fans. There are many who love it, but then there are many who criticize the title for various reasons. Some of the reasons include the messy controls, and the dislike of using FLUDD constantly.

However, there is a large fanbase who misses this game - and I am not just saying that because it is one of my favorite Mario games. I’ve talked to many people who have said that they would love to see a full remake of Super Mario Sunshine.

Plus, remaking the game would allow Nintendo to fix some of the issues that it has. The team could make FLUDD more entertaining to use, fix the messy controls, and update the core gameplay to better fit the newer Mario titles.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may be the most beloved Zelda title out there, but The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask is a close second, with many fans saying they love it almost as much as Ocarina of Time.

Majora’s Mask is the edgy older brother of Ocarina of Time, giving players a darker story that is full of twists and turns. Plus, it is a direct sequel to Ocarina of Time, so it feels like a no-brainer to continue making remakes by giving Majora’s Mask the treatment given to its little brother.

After seeing Ocarina of Time in this new light, fans would go crazy if they could play the game’s sequel shortly after. There are plenty of other Zelda games worth revisiting, too.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

If there are two Pokémon games that I hear mentioned all the time, they are Pokémon Colosseum and Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness. Gale of Darkness is the one I played a lot as a child, and is also typically the one I hear people talk about more.

Of course, both of these games deserve the Ocarina of Time treatment, but I think that Gale of Darkness deserves it a bit more. This game is one of the best Pokémon spin-offs, with it focusing on an evil organization that is creating shadow Pokémon.

More importantly, they created a Shadow Lugia and want to take over the world. Along with an actual evil organization, the game features a fun battle system that could use some updating to make it more modern. Plus, they could add all of the Pokémon to the game to make things more interesting.

Back in the days of the GameBoy Color, there were two titles that were ahead of their time. I am, of course, referring to The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Ages and Oracle of Seasons. Both were fantastic titles for the time.

The best part about them is that they were linked together, expanding the story for those who played through both of them. When you beat one, you got a password. When you typed that password into the other game, it linked the two. When you beat the second title, it gives you a password to take back into the first game. This allows you to get the true ending.

It was an interesting mechanic that games didn’t typically do back then. Now, if Nintendo brings these titles back, makes them 3D or HD-2D, then the fan base would go wild and buy both of them. Plus, new technology means you can link the saves without the need of a password.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

One of the classic platformers from the N64 era is none other than Donkey Kong 64. It is a beloved title that could seriously use updating. After all, the Nintendo 64 wasn’t known for being the smoothest gameplay, and that is prevalent with DK64.

Despite the clunkiness, there is a huge soft spot for this title, and it is one that brings the entire crew together, allowing you to play as DK, Diddy, Lanky, Chunky, and more.

Nintendo brought back the idea of Donkey Kong being in a 3D platformer with Donkey Kong Bananza in June 2025, and it sold decently well, revealing that players still enjoy seeing this ape in his own games. If Nintendo wants to keep bringing back the classics, then this should be a serious consideration.

Earthbound is not a game that I personally grew up with, but it is one that I have always been told to try, and one that I know means a lot to the Nintendo fan base. I’ve met individuals who play it on a yearly basis because of how much they love it. It remains one of the memorable SNES role-playing games.

With all that being said, the game could use some serious updating. Its old-school RPG turn-based combat doesn’t hold up to today’s standard. Imagine if Nintendo gave this game the HD-2D treatment, or even decided to make the game fully 3D.

Either way, it would look fantastic, and it would mean the world to those who grew up with this beloved title and played it since then.

The first of the Fire Emblem games to be released in the west was simply titled Fire Emblem, but it is also known as Fire Emblem: The Blazing Blade, and it follows the story of Lyn, Eliwood, and Hector.

I remember getting this game as a child and falling in love with it. Since then, Fire Emblem has become one of my favorite game series from Nintendo. There are many who say that Path of Radiance is their favorite game, and it holds up well, but if Nintendo is going to go down the remake route, I think it would be best to start with the first game that was brought over to the west. This is just one highlight of many excellent Fire Emblem games.

The Fire Emblem series has seen some great success, with the latest of the games - Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave - selling over 1.3 million copies in a month. It is a series that has been beloved for decades, and it deserves to see one of the earlier titles brought back in either HD-2D or full 3D like the modern games.

There is no doubt that one of the most popular games Nintendo has ever made is Super Mario 64, and it has a special place in history. This game set the standards for movement and camera control in a 3D space.

Super Mario 64 is one of the most well-known games that was released on the N64, with it only being second to maybe Ocarina of Time. Not only that, but it inspired multiple games that came after.

If there is any game that Nintendo has created outside of The Legend of Zelda series that deserves a full remake with modernized graphics, it would be Super Mario 64. Almost any fan of Nintendo would say that a remake of this game would be a no-brainer.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4244. How To Unlock Every The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Song

Music obviously plays a major role in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while most of the Ocarina songs will be mandatorily taught to Link for story progression, there are a few that can be missed entirely.

The optional songs include some secrets and quality-of-life perks that might help you out as you complete the main story, so be sure to grab all of them as soon as you can!

All of these songs are learned through story progression, so you do not need to personally seek them out. They are required for various story tasks and the game will lead you to them when the time is right. You will need all of these songs to reach the end of the game.

Impa will give Link this song after meeting Zelda for the first time at Hyrule Castle.

A cheerful tune that connects to Saria and makes Darunia dance.

After reaching Goron City, you'll be led into the Lost Forest and guided by a song to the Sacred Grove. There, you'll find Saria, who will teach you this song.

Stir space and time with this miraculous tune.

Automatically learned when you obtain the Ocarina of Time at Hyrule Castle.

Control the elements of wind and water with this little ditty.

Learned inside the Windmill in Kakariko Village.

Play this mystical tune to travel to the Sacred Grove.

Learned after visiting the Sacred Grove as Adult Link.

Travel to Death Mountain Crater by playing this fiery song.

Taught by Sheik after Adult Link visits Death Mountain Crater.

This whimsical melody will take you to Lake Hylia.

Unlocked after completing the Ice Cavern.

Whisk away to the Evil Desert Colossus with this powerful song.

Taught by Sheik after you reach Evil Desert Colossus for the first time.

Play this uplifting tune to travel to the Temple of Time.

Learned in the Temple of Time after completing the Forest Temple.

Here is how to complete the Water Temple in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

Most songs are taught to Link naturally through the story, but if you venture off the beaten path, you can find a few optional songs. These songs aren't required for progression, but do make navigating Hyrule a bit easier.

While in Kakariko Village, head into the Graveyard, down the path to the right of the windmill. At the back of the Graveyard, you'll find a Triforce symbol on the ground. Play Zelda's Lullaby there to open the Royal Tomb, where you'll find the Sun Song.

Play this song to summon Epona, Link's horse.

The first time you visit Hyrule Castle, you'll find a girl named Malon sitting outside the castle gate, waiting for her papa. She'll ask for your help waking up her dad, who she assumes has fallen asleep, and give you an egg that will hatch into a Wake-Up Cucco. Use this Cucco to wake up her dad when you find him inside the castle gates.

Once you leave Hyrule Castle, they will have returned to Lon Lon Ranch. Exit the castle and head to the ranch in the middle of the field, where you can find Malon towards the back, with some horses. She'll introduce you to Epona and mention that there's a song that helps calm them. Pull out the Ocarina, and she'll teach you Epona's song.

Play whenever you see out-of-reach areas with straw floating around in the wind. It will summon Pierre, whom you can then use with your Hookshot.

Once you reach Lake Hylia after diving in the Zora Domain, you'll find two scarecrows along the lake's edge. The scarecrows are named Pierre and Bonooru. If you approach Pierre, he'll ask you to play a song for him. There's no specific song to play. All you need to do is make one up.

After you make up a song and play it, press 'ok' and Pierre will dance to your song. Once it's over, Pierre will instruct you to play it for Bonooru, who will memorize it.

At this point, wait until you're able to return to these Scarecrows as adult Link, then play it for them again. This will fully unlock the song and the ability to use it.

Here is where to find all 36 Pieces of Heart in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

#4243. Shigeru Miyamoto Proclaims November 1 is Pikmin Day, Pikmin 4 Demo Coming To Switch 2 Soon

This morning, Nintendo shared some updates related to the Pikmin franchise and has officially claimed November 1 as Pikmin Day, starting today and moving forward presumably forever.

Aside from the announcement of Pikmin Day as a general idea, Pikmin creator Shigeru Miyamoto appeared on camera to remind everyone that Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is coming November 12. A free demo for the game, which will include one standard level and two Dandori Academy levels, will be available on November 2.

The Switch 2 version of the game (you can read Game Informer’s Pikmin 4 review here) will have improved visuals and take advantage of the Switch 2’s mic to let you say things like “Rush” and “Go to work” to Oatchi. The Dandori Academy side of the game is essentially time trials you can practice, and then on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, you will have one chance to post your best time. You can read more about the Switch 2 version of the game here.

Miyamoto also shared that the mobile game, Pikmin Bloom, is also getting a fairly substantial update soon with secret caves. In Bloom, players will be able to find maps that reveal caves that you can send your Pikmin into to battle and find treasure. You can also find maps for Bloom by playing Pikmin 4. Caves will be coming to Pikmin Bloom later this year.

The Pikmin Day presentation also reminded viewers that every Pikmin game is available on Switch and Switch 2, though no announcements or hints were made implying that Pikmin 1 and 2 would be coming to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service, which includes GameCube games on Switch 2. Those games can be purchased individually on the eShop.

Finally, Miyamoto brought actress Fuka Koshiba on the presentation (best known for voicing Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service) to share her appreciation for the Pikmin franchise (she likes to knit Pikmin hats that she shares on social media) and introduce a Pikmin short film. In the short, a Pikmin interacts with a toad, but I won’t spoil what happens. Miyamoto promised more shorts are on the way and in the future, they will be found in the Nintendo Today app.

Unfortunately, the stream concluded without a single reference to 2017's Hey! Pikmin. I wouldn't expect it to get a port to Switch 2 anytime soon.

#4242. Yakuza Creator Toshiro Nagoshi's Studio Has Officially Shut Down, Ending Gang Of Dragon's Development With It

Nagoshi Studio, the developer led by Yakuza/Like a Dragon series creator Toshiro Nagoshi, has officially shut down, ending development of Gang of Dragon, which was revealed at The Game Awards last year. Shareholders resolved to dissolve the studio on October 31, according to a notice published in a Japanese government newspaper called Kanpo, as first reported by Gematsu.

This follows a report from Bloomberg earlier this year that said Chinese gaming megacorp NetEase Games was cutting funding to Nagoshi Studio, allowing Nagoshi to seek independent funding elsewhere. It seems he couldn't find funding, and now Nagoshi Studio is no more. NetEase helped Nagoshi found the studio in November 2021.

You can watch the Gang of Dragon reveal trailer below for a look at what the team was cooking up:

This closure follows other signals that NetEase is looking to divest from the gaming scene outside of its Chinese studios. A little over a month ago, Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture left NetEase to go independent again, just months after the launch of Romeo Is A Dead Man.

#4241. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

If you’re just getting started in Crimson Desert yourself, or plan to do so soon, we recommend reading these crucial tips to help orient yourself in the game’s vast world. You should also plan your initial skill unlocks by prioritising these skills to spend your Abyss Artifacts first.

It doesn't seem to be slowing down, either. In its latest financial results briefing, Nintendo has now shared a reminder about some of the titles coming to the system over the next year. This includes games like Final Fantasy VII Revelation and FromSoft's Switch 2 exclusive The Duskbloods, which was recently delayed.

Here are Nintendo's highlights. Layton's new outing and a few other titles also get a shoutout, as late 2026 arrivals.

"More third-party multiplatform titles coming to Nintendo on day one, in addition to titles developed for Nintendo Switch 2"

Nintendo has also used this opportunity to share some charts, illustrating how third-party continues to provide support for overall software sales on the Switch and Switch 2. It also plays a major role in driving engagement.

"Ongoing sales of our previously released evergreen titles, together with sales of third-party titles, provide substantial support for overall software unit sales.

"...Titles from software publishers account for a significant share of software unit sales, making a substantial contribution to our business. Furthermore, their software has a strong presence among download-only titles, which are not included in this graph, and plays a major role in sustaining engagement with our hardware."

On the first-party front, Nintendo has this week reconfirmed the release windows for multiple upcoming Switch 2 titles. You can find out what else is on the way in our previous story.

#4239. Where To Find All Great Fairies In The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

The Great Fairies are a staple of the Zelda franchise, but especially The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. While they might all look the same, rest assured that there are six unique Great Fairies across Hyrule with gifts to grant Link.

That said, these gifts don't come free, so if you're hoping to take advantage of everything the Great Fairies have to offer, then you'll need to start saving up your Rupees for offerings now.

You don't need to find the Great Fairies in any particular order, and you don't have to accept every gift. The most natural order follows the locations you'll visit throughout the story, in order, but you can visit and accept the gifts in any order once you have access to the areas.

Found at the top of Death Mountain, after completing the Dodongo Cavern dungeon and helping Goron City.

Din's Fire: Create a fiery dome around you when you cast. Uses 2 Magic Power.

After passing through the gate on the path to Zelda, you'll see a short path off to the right with a breakable rock wall. Use a bomb to clear the way to this Great Fairy.

Improved Spin: Strike nearby foes with a mighty wave of magic power. You will be vulnerable while charging it up.

After you give King Zora the letter, you'll gain access to the Zora Fountain. In this area, head to the island at the southern end of the map to find the Great Fairy's entrance.

Farore's Wind: Create a waypoint you can warp to when in a dungeon. Uses 2 Magic Power.

After beating the Fire Temple, you can find this entrance in the Death Mountain Crater, south on the map of the path that leads back to Goron City.

Doubled Magic: Permanently doubles your pool of magic power.

Once you reach the Desert Colossus, look for the breakable wall on the northern part of the map.

Nayru's Love: Grants invulnerability when cast. Uses 4 Magic Power.

After you obtain the Golden Gauntlets inside Ganondorf's Castle, head back out through the entrance and look for the side path with the Great Fairy's entrance that you should now be able to clear.

Halved Damage: Permanently halves the damage taken from foes.

Here is where to locate all 100 Gold Skulltulas and what you get for your efforts in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

#4237. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.

#4236. Ori Creator Is Very Unhappy With How Nintendo Handled Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

We all know that few games have left as lasting an impression on the gaming industry as The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Even decades after its original release, the Nintendo classic continues to inspire developers and entire generations of players.

And its recently released remake has already brought plenty of attention back to Hyrule, with many critics and players praising its beautiful new presentation and sharing emotional reactions to revisiting one of their favorite adventures – no wonder it’s already one of the highest-rated games ever!

However, not everyone is completely satisfied with Nintendo's approach. Thomas Mahler, best known as the creator of the acclaimed Ori franchise, has shared a rather lengthy criticism of the remake on X (formerly Twitter), explaining why he believes the developer missed an opportunity to make the experience much better from a game design perspective.

Mahler recently shared his thoughts on social media after playing the Ocarina of Time remake alongside his son, who was immediately impressed by its new art direction. The developer even mentioned that his son was so amazed by the visuals that he tried touching the screen to grab the Kokiri Sword when he first obtained it, which is pretty cute!

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

Unfortunately, Mahler himself wasn't nearly as impressed with the experience. In his post, he curiously explained that he has always been somewhat disappointed by the original Ocarina of Time, particularly when comparing it to A Link to the Past. For him, the Nintendo 64 adventure feels emptier and more confusing, and the problem now is that the remake hasn't addressed those issues.

Thomas Mahler, best known as the creator of the acclaimed Ori franchise, has shared a rather lengthy criticism of the remake, explaining why he believes the developer missed an opportunity to make the experience much better from a game design perspective.

His biggest complaint revolves around Hyrule Field, which he considers one of the game's weakest areas. Mahler believes its relatively empty design was understandable back in 1998, considering the Nintendo 64's technical limitations. However, with modern hardware and the technology available today, he feels Nintendo could have done much more than simply improve its appearance. “Sure, Hyrule Field looks prettier now, but it's still just as empty and uninteresting as it was back then,” Mahler explained.

Mahler believes the remake could have taken a similar approach to A Link to the Past by introducing more activities, hidden areas, and interactions throughout Hyrule Field. He also suggested that acquiring new dungeon items should encourage players to revisit previously explored locations and discover paths or secrets they couldn't access before.

Instead, he feels Nintendo preserved an outdated design that could have benefited from a more substantial overhaul. He even argued that the game would deserve a 7.5 or 8 out of 10 today, rather than the perfect scores some reviewers have awarded it.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Naturally, Mahler's comments didn't go unnoticed, and plenty of Zelda fans pushed back against his opinion. Some questioned whether changing the original game's structure would undermine what made Ocarina of Time so special in the first place.

The developer wasn't particularly convinced by those arguments, however, and continued defending his position in the replies. “Let's be a bunch of bozos instead who praise 1998 game design and act like it's the end all be all even though Nintendo themselves would never ever design a shit overworld like that for their next mainline entry," he responded.

It's worth noting that Mahler did acknowledge the remake's impressive visuals, and his criticism is primarily directed at its level design rather than its presentation. Still, his comments highlight an interesting discussion about how much developers should change when revisiting beloved classics.

After all, preserving what made a game special and improving the elements that haven't aged quite as well aren't necessarily mutually exclusive. And while plenty of players are clearly enjoying their return to Hyrule, Mahler's reaction shows that even a legendary adventure like Ocarina of Time won't be everyone's cup of tea.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4235. Nintendo To Continue Delivering Movies Beyond Live-Action Zelda, Unsurprisingly

Nintendo is now fully committed to the movie business thanks to Super Mario and the upcoming live-action Zelda film, due out 30th April 2027.

During the latest financial briefing, company president Shuntaro Furukawa has reiterated how the Japanese firm intends to "continue delivering movies" with its partners beyond the Zelda film - while also reassuring fans that each film will be "carefully" crafted.

The plan is to also establish a "framework", allowing for ongoing production. Here's the graphic attached to these comments:

"As announced, a live-action movie of The Legend of Zelda is scheduled for release in 2027, and we plan to continue delivering movies in the years that follow.

"We will work with our partners to carefully craft each film, while establishing a framework that supports ongoing production."

The Galaxy Movie has already provided enough evidence of another Mario movie, but Nintendo hasn't officially said anything.

There have also been some rumours about the Zelda movie going beyond a single film, but the first one still needs to come out (and make bank at the global box office).

Furukawa has also issued a reminder about how the combined worldwide box office sales of the animated Mario Movies have now exceeded two billion US dollars, further expanding Nintendo's reach to new audiences and regions.

"We believe these movies have provided an opportunity for people to get to know Mario, including people in regions where our dedicated video game platform business has had limited reach and people who do not normally play games."

#4234. The Elder Scrolls VI Has An Official Subtitle And It's 'Sentinel'

The headline tells the story: The Elder Scrolls VI has an official subtitle and it's Sentinel. So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The news comes from Bethesda's various social media accounts, which are all sharing the video above. Along with the video, music, and the title, it also shares the text as a quote attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest to High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell (4E 206): "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Sentinel is one of the nine major kingdoms within Hammerfell and is the capital of both the Alik'r Desert region and the Myrkwasa region of the Alik'r (source: elderscrolls.fandom). With this knowledge, it's fair to assume Sentinel will have many desert locations.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4233. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4232. Petit Planet’s Gacha System Will Only be For Cosmetics

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

HoYoVerse’s bread and butter is, of course, gacha games. From its first big hit in Honkai Impact 3rd to the breakout success of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero, gacha is what brings home the bacon. The items distributed through these games’ gacha banners usually include characters, weapons, equipment, and other assorted elements that directly impact your experience with the game. If you want to play, you gotta be willing to roll the dice.

With the looming release of Petit Planet, HoYo’s new Animal Crossing-style life sim game, players have been curious as to how, exactly, the gacha element will factor into this particular style of game. It’d be pretty lousy, for example, if you had to keep rolling on banners just to see all of the game’s villagers and experience their stories.

The new life sim gacha game is launching ahead of several other titles this winter.

However, in a departure from its established formula, HoYo’s actually taking a slightly different approach to monetization in Petit Planet. There will still be a gacha system, of course, but the only items this gacha will dispense will be strictly cosmetic, with all of the actual gameplay stuff being readily accessible to everyone whether they’re willing to roll or not.

At the HoYoverse Media Tour 2026 in Seoul, South Korea, two representatives from the Petit Planet dev team, lead game designer Murphy and lead artist Yinli Huang, explained their philosophy to the surrounding press.

In an interview with gaming outlet Geek Culture, Murphy explained that, rather than paywalling access to the game’s content through gacha banners or direct purchases, the goal is to make all of the actual gameplay elements available to all players, with whatever paid elements there being strictly limited to extra cosmetic stuff like character outfits and furniture.

“All of Petit Planet’s core gameplay, including its life simulation and all content related to forming friendships and building stories with the Neighbours, is included for all free players,” Murphy said. “In terms of our monetisation model, we can confirm that it will only be associated with cosmetics, meaning things like furniture and clothes.”

The goal is to make all of the actual gameplay elements available to all players.

This is quite a departure from HoYo’s other major titles. I play Honkai: Star Rail, for example, and because I don’t have every single character and all of their optimal gacha-earned equipment, I’m basically locked out of the game’s hardest endgame game modes.

Wuthering Waves is one of the biggest Gachas on the planet, and they do far better than most at answering player complaints. Let's go over exactly how!

Petit Planet is slated to specifically be a cozy life sim game rather than a management life sim. Many games of this genre purport to be cozy, but because they demand such constant, consistent engagement from you, they kind of stop being cute little daily life simulators and start being second jobs. The dev team is hoping to use the game’s live-service model to offer consistent, interesting content to the players without directly stoking FOMO.

“As a live-service title, we will constantly add new content to the game, like festival events, which are inspired by real-world festivals, alongside the concept of seasons,” Murphy told Geek Culture. “Each season, players will be able to meet new Neighbours, alongside new clothes and furniture to unlock.”

The crux of this pursuit is an as-of-yet undetermined system that would allow players to properly experience and reap the benefits of seasons’ past even if they weren’t playing the game at the time. Again, Star Rail does regular time-limited events, and while they all offer limited-time currency rewards, the actual gameplay elements remain accessible long after their endpoints. Even so, Murphy wants these types of events in Petit Planet to be as low-pressure as possible so players are interested without feeling obligated.

“We always come back to the randomness in daily life, so there’s no growth curve in our game, we just want to provide more of those little surprises and small pleasures in life for players.”

We were able to get some extensive time with HoYoverse's upcoming life simulator, Petit Planet, and were left grinning from ear-to-ear.

#4231. YouTuber Finds Ocarina Of Time Remake Dialogue Tied To A Majora's Mask Amiibo

It has been four days since the Ocarina of Time remake was released, and dedicated fans have already made some fascinating discoveries. Not just easter eggs and subtle differences between the remake and the original, but hidden dialogue that many think suggests a Majora’s Mask remake is already in the works.

YouTuber Austin John Plays has posted a video in which he shares the codes for the upcoming Ocarina remake amiibo. The Young Link and Young Zelda amiibo, which will be released in 2027, seemingly to coincide with the launch of The Legend of Zelda movie, unlock in-game masks of the characters’ original N64 designs when scanned.

Those amiibo have the codes Mask 101 and Mask 102, but upon discovering this, John also found a third, unannounced amiibo with the code Mask 103. There is naturally no image of the mask tied to its codename; however, as is the case with the two announced masks, there are lines of dialogue attached to it.

NPCs will react to Link in unique ways if you approach them wearing the N64 masks when you can unlock them next year. It’s the lines of dialogue attached to that third mask that make it seem like we’re getting at least one more Ocarina remake amiibo, and the conclusion John and his viewers have reached is that somehow, some way, we’re getting a Majora’s Mask remake.

The dialogue attached to Mask 103 all boils down to those who see it being afraid of it, referring to it as weird, strange, and creepy. Noted in a Reddit thread covering John’s findings, one of the lines of dialogue attached to the mask comments on it scaring away monsters from whoever’s wearing it. That’s how Majora’s Mask functions in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

My takeaway from that is that we will perhaps get a Skull Kid amiibo down the line that unlocks Majora’s Mask in the Ocarina of Time remake, and that wearing the mask will effectively unlock an easy mode where monsters are too afraid to attack you. However, most people think there’s more to it, especially since Majora’s Mask was the original Ocarina’s sequel.

If you’re not a little skeptical about all of this, like I am, then you seem to fall into one of two camps. Either you believe this discovery proves a Majora’s Mask remake is coming, or that this suggests it will be DLC rather than a full-blown remake sequel.

Despite my skepticism, I do think it would be a little silly of Nintendo if its next Zelda project isn't a Majora’s Mask remake. I’d also understand why it might want to give it a miss, or relegate it to Ocarina DLC. Majora’s Mask didn’t have nearly as big a cultural impact as Ocarina, so despite the overall success of Zelda in 2026, Nintendo might still be a little worried that a standalone Majora’s Mask remake might not have the same cache that Ocarina of Time carries.

#4230. You Can Preload Grand Theft Auto VI On PS5 and Xbox Next Week, And You'll Want To Because It's Massive

We're just over two weeks away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which recently graced the cover of Game Informer. Ahead of its November 19 launch, Rockstar Games has announced that digital preloading for GTA VI will begin next week on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

More specifically, preloading on Xbox Series X/S will begin Tuesday, November 10, at 12 a.m. GMT (4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on November 9), and on PS5 at midnight local time in your time zone. Although Rockstar isn't producing physical discs of GTA VI, you can still buy a physical box at retail, which includes a download code for the game. The studio says, "Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12."

The preload file will require 212 GB on your device, so make sure you have the space before you start the download. You can find more details about this process here.

Elsewhere in today's GTA VI news, Rockstar has revealed that on November 19, it will add an official printable GTA VI cover art poster and a map of Leonida as a free digital download to the game's official site. However, a double-sided physical version of this poster will be made available shortly after the launch of GTA VI from the Rockstar Store. It will only cost $0.99 on its own, or come free with any other purchase from the store.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. After that, check out this exclusive story about how GTA VI features over 170 animal species and another about how the game features tropical storms and hurricanes.

#4229. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

#4227. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.
